Human creativity is an integral part of our daily lives, yet the computational analysis of creative thinking remains an underexplored area. Among the most intriguing forms of human creativity is the ability to compare seemingly disparate things - a fundamental aspect of our understanding. This paper focuses on visual metaphor detection as a way to study creative comparison, and presents a new, high-precision dataset that offers a more comprehensive view of this phenomenon. This dataset, known as MetaCLUE, is the result of manually annotating a substantial collection of images, each with multiple, diverse comparisons. By examining the performance of existing state-of-the-art models on MetaCLUE at three different levels - object, attribute, and scene - the study highlights the need for more detailed, challenging datasets to support the development of more accurate visual metaphor detection models. Furthermore, the study identifies areas for improvement in future research, including the investigation of more complex, multi-sourced comparisons and the integration of linguistic information to enhance the accuracy of visual metaphor detection. Specifically, we demonstrate that the topological Betti numbers of $X$ can be calculated by analyzing the Hilbert series of the cohomology ring of $\pi_1(X)$, considered as a free module over the polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[e_1^{\pm}, \ldots, e_k^{\pm}]$. This result is established through an isomorphism between the cohomology ring and the ring of $X$-valued valuations on $\mathbb{Z}[t_1^{\pm}, \ldots, t_k^{\pm}]$, which is achieved by constructing a non-archimedean valuation on any non-trivial loop in $\pi_1(X)$. Additionally, we show that the Hilbert series of the cohomology ring of $\pi_1(X)$ is a polynomial in $e_1^{\pm}, \ldots, e_k^{\pm}$, and that it encodes the Betti numbers of $X$ as its coefficients. We introduce a novel online algorithm called dART, designed to tackle the non-linear top-K subset identification issue. This issue requires selecting the top-K subgroups with the highest underlying parameters, where each subgroup's parameter is drawn from a non-linear distribution. Our algorithm is built upon the classical adaptive reject accept algorithm, which has been proven to be asymptotically optimal for linear models. However, its performance is limited in non-linear scenarios, prompting the development of dART. This algorithm adapts the reject strategy based on the current estimate of the parameter distribution, which is incrementally updated via a Bayesian approach. Our analysis demonstrates that dART achieves a sublinear error rate in estimating the parameter distribution, under which we show its ability to identify the top-K subgroups with a nearly optimal number of samples. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive simulation study to validate the efficacy of dART. Our algorithm's performance is further demonstrated in a real-world study examining the effects of air pollution on infant mortality rates. Our results reveal significant differences in the underlying parameters across subgroups, underscoring the importance of subgroup analysis in non-linear models. Moreover, we apply dART to identify the top-K subgroups with the highest per capita healthcare expenditures in the US. Our findings highlight the disparities in healthcare spending between subgroups, which is consistent with previous research in the field. Our algorithm's versatility is also showcased in its application to the group-wise regression coefficient identification issue. Our results demonstrate that dART achieves state-of-the-art performance in both non-linear and linear scenarios, outperforming competing algorithms like RRT and the Bayesian optimization-based approach, which is computationally more expensive due to its Monte Carlo Bayesian optimization procedure. Overall, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of dART in identifying subgroups with a large number of samples, while achieving a nearly optimal error rate in the process. This study underscores the importance of subgroup analysis in non-linear models, which is a critical consideration in many scientific domains. Our findings are expected to facilitate the development of more efficient algorithms for non-linear issues, which is a pressing challenge in the statistics community. The efficiency of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) is significantly influenced by the number of filters, which are the core components of convolutional layers.  However, the high computational cost and large memory requirements of filters can hinder the use of CNNs on devices with limited computational capabilities.  To overcome this challenge, researchers have been exploring filter pruning techniques that involve automatically removing unnecessary filters from the network.  This approach can be used to reduce the size of CNNs and make them compatible with devices that have low computational capabilities.  This paper introduces a novel Self Similarity Matrix based filter pruning method that uses a similarity metric to evaluate filters and eliminate the least similar ones.  The proposed method is based on the self-similarity of visual scenes, which is an inherent property of CNNs.  The method is evaluated on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets with different pruning strategies and compared with other state-of-the-art techniques.  The results show that the proposed method achieves a high accuracy of 92.2% on the CIFAR-10 dataset while reducing the number of filters by 85% compared to a baseline model.  The analysis of the pruning algorithm's convergence and the sensitivity of the similarity metric to hyper-parameters is also provided. It presents a novel approach that trains models in stages, starting with a general model that generalizes well across multiple datasets, then fine-tuning a model trained on one dataset to optimize performance on another, and repeating this process on a new dataset. Experimental results using the CUB200-2011 dataset and the BirdCLEF 2021 dataset show that this two-stage transfer learning method outperforms single-stage models trained from scratch, and a three-stage approach achieves superior results when compared to the two-stage method. Furthermore, the research compares the performance of pre-trained models trained on the ImageNet dataset with those trained on the bird datasets, revealing that the bird datasets are more suitable for pre-training high-performing models. Additionally, the study evaluates the impact of data augmentation techniques on model performance and compares the results with those obtained by other researchers using the same dataset. All code and models used in this research are publicly available on the GitHub repository named "Birds-Classification". The final results are presented in a table and figure. Cache side-channel attacks have been identified as a threat to software security, as they can be exploited to extract sensitive information. These attacks are particularly challenging to detect as they can be hidden from standard security tools. To address this issue, our research introduces a novel approach for tracking and pinpointing cache side-channel vulnerabilities in software. The method is based on a new algorithm that analyzes the timing patterns of a program's context switches. It has been tested on various open-source and proprietary software and has successfully identified 5 distinct cache side-channel vulnerabilities in 3 separate programs. These vulnerabilities were then validated by conducting controlled attacks using the analyzed timing patterns. The results of this research demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in detecting cache side-channel vulnerabilities in real-world software. Our work contributes to the justice-focused discourse on algorithmic systems by identifying key findings and recommending strategies to mitigate harm, which include involving research participants in decision-making processes and prioritizing equity in algorithmic design. Furthermore, our study highlights the need for a more inclusive and participatory approach to developing algorithms and provides a framework for justice in algorithmic misinformation detection, which emphasizes the importance of human-centered design and equitable research practices. Ultimately, our work aims to inspire further research on the justice implications of algorithms and promote the development of more humane technology. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have gained immense popularity in generating high-quality synthetic data that closely resembles real-world data. However, the unstable nature of GAN training poses significant challenges. One of the primary reasons for this instability is mode collapse, a common problem that occurs when a GAN fails to produce diverse samples, resulting in convergence to a limited subset of the data distribution. To address mode collapse, researchers have employed various techniques, including data augmentation and multi-scale architectures. This study leverages the concept of differentiability to investigate mode collapse. Specifically, we analyze the Hessian of the generator's loss function, which represents the local curvature, or second derivative, of the data distribution. By examining Hessian eigenvalues, we can determine the extent of mode collapse, as a lower value indicates a stronger correlation between different modes and a more gradual transition between them. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing metrics in identifying mode collapse, especially in complex datasets. Furthermore, we show that using Hessian eigenvalues can improve the stability of GAN training, leading to better mode collapse prevention and higher Inception Score. The proposed method is also found to be computationally efficient, requiring minimal memory and time. The accompanying code is available on GitHub. The recent development of the CLIP model has led to significant advancements in the field of computer vision, enabling the learning of visual representations through self-supervised learning. However, the existing CLIP model is limited in its ability to adapt to new domains, as it requires extensive retraining. To overcome this limitation, we propose a domain prompt learning framework that enables the adaptation of the pre-trained CLIP model to new domains, significantly reducing the retraining time. Our proposed method involves generating a domain prompt for each new domain, which is achieved by fine-tuning the CLIP model on a small dataset of 100 images per domain, using a contrastive learning objective. This allows the CLIP model to adapt to new domains, while maintaining its performance on the original domain, resulting in a substantial reduction in retraining time. Our proposed method has been extensively tested and validated on various benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in adapting the CLIP model to new domains. Our results show that the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SimCLR and WebImageText benchmarks, while significantly reducing the retraining time by a factor of 10. Our code has been made publicly available for further research and development. The code can be found at the GitHub repository located at https://github.com/zhilin-you/Domain-Prompt-CLIP. The associated dataset is available at https://github.com/zhilin-you/Domain-Prompt-CLIP-Data. The pre-trained model is available at https://huggingface.co/dompromptclips. The pre-trained model has been fine-tuned on the ImageNet dataset and has been adapted to various downstream domains, allowing for efficient fine-tuning on new tasks. Our research has been published in the paper titled "Domain Prompt Learning for Adapting CLIP to Unseen Domains" and is accepted for publication in the 31st ACM International Conference on Multimedia, 2023. Deep learning models have become increasingly vulnerable to stealthy attacks that manipulate predictions without being detected. A particularly insidious form of such an attack is the backdoor attack, where malicious input triggers incorrect model outputs without raising suspicion. Existing countermeasures often rely on specific knowledge about the attack or model architecture, limiting their effectiveness. Our research introduces DeepPayload, a novel black-box backdoor attack that exploits deep learning models through neural payload injection, injecting a stealthy trigger into the model's neural activity. By employing a gradient-based optimization technique, DeepPayload successfully injects the trigger without altering the model's original functionality, even across different model architectures. In experiments involving multiple image classification models, DeepPayload demonstrated impressive injection success rates of up to 100\%, with impressive attack success rates reaching 100\% on certain models. Our study also shows that DeepPayload can successfully attack models with which it was not trained and did not have access to model weights. Our findings highlight the need for more robust defenses against sophisticated attacks that can manipulate deep learning models without being detected. Recent advancements in deep neural networks have significantly improved the performance of traditional survival analysis models. However, the lack of interpretable explanations for their predictions remains a major challenge, particularly when it comes to complex deep survival models. In response, we introduce the Reverse Survival Model (RSM), a novel pipeline that can provide insights into the predictions made by these models. RSM uses a unique combination of techniques, including the "reverse fitting" method and gradient-based optimization, to identify the most important factors contributing to patient outcomes. By employing this approach, RSM can explain not only the final predictions made by a deep survival model, but also the underlying factors that lead to them throughout the patient's follow-up period. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RSM on two publicly available datasets, showing that it can provide valuable explanations for the predictions made by deep survival models while minimizing the risk of overfitting to the specific model used. This study investigates the asymptotic properties of the spatial integration of the solution to a modified heat equation on a torus, which incorporates time-invariant noise. We establish a central limit theorem for the integrated solution under two scenarios: when the noise on the torus can be broken down into its Fourier components with slowly decaying coefficients, and when the noise on the torus exhibits certain properties known as $\alpha$-Hölder regularity and large-scale behavior. We show that these integrated solutions converge to specific Gaussian distributions at an exponential rate, which is crucial for the validity of our findings. The results in this study encompass both cases of noise that are and are not smooth, making it a first that such an approach has been achieved simultaneously for these two cases. The study also includes numerical simulations to verify the theoretical results in this research. This research presents a hierarchical control framework for quadruped robots to achieve simultaneous locomotion and manipulation over varied terrain. The core issue is developing an efficient control system that can adapt to changing conditions to ensure reliable locomotion and accurate manipulation. To address this challenge, a hierarchical control structure is proposed, consisting of two layers: a lower level controlling foot movement and an upper level managing upper limb movements in relation to the body's position. The foot level control employs a model-based predictive control approach to optimize foot placement, taking into account terrain constraints, to enhance overall system performance. The upper level control uses a feedback control model to stabilize the body position, allowing the lower level to dynamically adjust the foot movement for stable body orientation. The stability of the control system is mathematically proven, and the effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through simulations and experiments on the Cypress robot, showcasing its ability to adapt to uneven terrain and manipulate objects in real-world scenarios. The presented hierarchical control framework successfully enables the Cypress robot to achieve stable and accurate manipulation over varied terrain without the need for external assistance. This research investigates the stable-matching Voronoi diagram, a variant of the traditional Voronoi diagram that assigns sites to points based on a stable matching algorithm. It presents two efficient algorithms: a randomized method with an expected time complexity of O(n^(1+2*ρ)) and a deterministic method with an time complexity of O(n^(2+2*ρ)), where ρ is between 1 and 2 and represents the dimensionality of the point set. Additionally, we demonstrate that a stable-matching Voronoi diagram can be constructed in O(n log n) time for ρ = 1. Our findings also establish a lower bound of Ω(n^(1+ρ)) for the combinatorial complexity of the diagram, confirming its representability by planar drawings with a restricted number of faces. Notably, our research resolves an open problem posed by Erickson in 2017. A stable-matching Delaunay triangulation is also introduced as a natural extension of the stable-matching Voronoi diagram. Our research provides a comprehensive framework for constructing these diagrams, accompanied by a set of experimental results that demonstrate their practical utility. This study presents a novel approach to pan-sharpening using an encoder-decoder structure with deep gradient projection neural networks. These networks, specifically designed for image reconstruction tasks, leverage gradient projection layers to optimize performance. By incorporating an L1 regularization loss, the proposed pan-sharpening method can effectively preserve detail in both spatial and spectral dimensions. Performance evaluations using satellite imagery from diverse sensors confirm the superior image quality achieved with this method, outshining existing pan-sharpening techniques. Associated source code is accessible via the GitHub repository 'gradientprojection', allowing for seamless reproduction of results. Successful applications include sharpening images obtained by the Constellations-2, Pléiades-A, WorldView-4, WorldView-3, GeoEye-1 and RapidEye-5.

The formation of amorphous carbon nanotubes is a widespread phenomenon observed in various experimental settings, yet it remains understudied compared to crystalline nanotubes. To investigate the connection between amorphous nanotube formation and random initial configurations, we conducted molecular dynamic simulations using two distinct systems: one featuring a disordered carbon sheet and the other a pre-existing nanotube. Both systems exhibited similar results, demonstrating that amorphous nanotubes can emerge from random configurations through a process of random diffusion and stress relaxation, with the initial structure's complexity and density influencing the nanotube's size and curvature. Notably, the nanotube's formation appears to be unrelated to pre-existing order within the random configuration. Furthermore, the simulations revealed that amorphous nanotubes can form through a random diffusion process, with the nanotube's curvature and size determined by local random configurations. These findings suggest that amorphous nanotube formation is a robust phenomenon that can occur from a wide range of random initial configurations. The study's results are supported by the observation that amorphous nanotubes are more resistant to defects and can form from random, defective structures. Overall, the findings of this research provide valuable insights into the amorphous nanotube formation mechanism and shed light on the properties of these unique materials. The research also has significant implications for understanding the properties of amorphous carbon materials. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been successfully applied to various natural language processing tasks, including text classification and node classification. However, the standard GNN method has significant drawbacks, including high computational complexity, large memory requirements, and limited scalability. To address these issues, a new propagation technique is proposed, which enables the reduction of computational and memory demands by limiting the propagation process to only the most relevant nodes. This approach is integrated into a novel GNN framework, called NODE-SELECT, and evaluated on four real-world text classification datasets. Comparative results show that NODE-SELECT outperforms standard GNN in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Additionally, the proposed framework's scalability is demonstrated on large datasets, confirming its potential to handle complex graph-based NLP tasks efficiently. Further analysis reveals that the selection of nodes in NODE-SELECT's propagation process is influenced by the distribution of semantic features within the graph. This insight is leveraged to develop a novel GNN framework, called NODE-SELECT-DF, which incorporates a dynamic selection strategy that adapts to changing graph topologies. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that NODE-SELECT-DF surpasses its predecessor in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Finally, the proposed frameworks are compared to state-of-the-art GNN models, revealing that they achieve comparable accuracy while significantly reducing complexity and computational demands. This breakthrough enables the efficient processing of large-scale graphs that are intractable to standard GNN models. Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) correlations are a key aspect of entanglement and nonlocality but distinguishing them from local randomness requires verifying that at least one party possesses more knowledge than the other, a phenomenon known as steering. To prove this, we have developed an experimental setup using single photons and a hybrid system, allowing us to establish a lower bound on the amount of information transmitted faster than light. By measuring the minimum distinguishable states, we have demonstrated that, even considering quantum-level local processing, Alice can transmit at least one bit of information beyond local capabilities to predict Bob's measurements, providing a concrete demonstration of faster-than-light information transmission in the context of EPR steering. This work highlights the necessity of faster-than-light information transmission for nonlocal phenomena like EPR correlations. Furthermore, our findings have implications for quantum network communication, as they suggest that, under certain conditions, Alice may be able to send information beyond local quantum network capabilities to predict Bob's measurements, a phenomenon that could potentially be exploited for local quantum network advantage in certain tasks. This research explores the relationship between gradient descent's convergence rate and the accuracy of statistical inference when applied to noisy optimization outcomes from linear regression, where the parameters are subject to differential privacy. Building upon prior work, we establish a convergence rate of O(n^(-1/2)) for the optimization process and O(n^(-1/4)) for the resulting estimates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these estimates can be effectively used for various statistical tests, achieving a critical threshold error probability and meeting the requirements of a natural test statistic. Our study also reveals the existence of a trade-off between the accuracy of the estimates and the test power. Additionally, we empirically confirm that the proposed method enables the utilization of standard statistical tools for differential privacy, ultimately allowing for meaningful interpretations of statistical results. Our research offers a novel perspective on the relationship between gradient descent and statistical estimation in private data analysis. We define intrinsic 3-linking in graphs, comprising two criteria: 
(1) graphs with a connected subgraph that includes all vertices and at least three edges, 
(2) graphs where short cycles of three edges form closed shapes. 
This study identifies spherical graphs that inherently meet these criteria, 
beginning with a complete enumeration of such graphs with at most 12 vertices. 
Additionally, we identify an infinite collection of intrinsic 3-linked graphs, 
composing the first verified examples of such graphs with more than 12 vertices. 
Furthermore, we demonstrate that a specific family of infinite graphs, 
comprising a sphere and two connected solid cylinders, 
is comprised entirely of intrinsic 3-linked graphs. 
Our work also explores the relationship between intrinsic 3-linking and another graph property, 
enlargement by a specific type of graph, 
and reveals a connection between these two characteristics. 
Finally, we examine the potential for graphs that are not inherently 3-linked to be made so through a specific transformation. 
Additionally, we discuss the challenge of categorizing all 3-linked graphs, 
and identify a method to simplify this task. 
This study provides a foundation for further research into intrinsic 3-linking in graphs, 
and offers insights into the broader study of intrinsic graph structures. 
In particular, it sheds light on the intrinsic graph structures of 3-dimensional manifolds. 
Moreover, it reveals a connection to the study of knot theory, 
enabling us to better understand the structure of 3-manifolds.

Our focus is on the sparse low-rank tensor regression problem, a challenging task in high-dimensional data analysis. Given a sparse tensor $x$ with $O(p)$ non-zero elements and a low rank $r$ tensor $A$, we investigate the tensor regression problem, a problem, whose existing algorithms often suffer from high computational complexity. In this work, a novel approach, called ISLET, is proposed, which leverages importance sampling and sketching to accelerate the computation of low-rank tensor regression. ISLET enjoys a significant improvement in computational complexity, reducing from $O(pgrb^2)$ to $O(pgr)$, and more importantly, it is statistically consistent in estimating the underlying tensor $x$ with a small sample size $n$. Theoretical analysis further confirms the optimality of ISLET's mean squared error under specific conditions. Experimental results also demonstrate the superiority of ISLET, both in terms of computational efficiency and estimation accuracy. The mechanical characteristics of soft tissues are typically described by the Mooney-Rivlin model, often considered a standard, yet it may not accurately represent all tissues. BCMS utilizes a Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm to determine the model parameters and determine the optimal model based on a Bayesian information criterion. When applied to biaxial testing data from porcine aortic valves, BCMS identified a finite deformation model that considers strain-dependent stiffness as the most accurate representation, significantly outperforming the Mooney-Rivlin model. This research highlights the importance of choosing the right constitutive model for a tissue, emphasizing the need to move beyond conventional models like the Mooney-Rivlin model. Traditional syndemic surveillance methods rely on specific disease patterns, but this approach is limited by its inability to adapt to outbreaks. Revising this method, we develop a more flexible system that identifies unusual events and generates alerts for general health concerns by analyzing overall pattern consistency in available data. This method was tested using US National Center for Health Monitoring's outpatient data and the results of a simulated influenza B outbreak indicate that it effectively detects anomalies and predicts trends, thereby facilitating early warning systems for a wide range of non-specific health events. This approach offers a potential alternative to traditional syndemic surveillance methods.

This problem is NP-hard and is inspired by a variant of the Maximal Independent Set Problem that employs quantum number coloring. We develop a new algorithm based on a tree search approach and demonstrate its ability to solve certain instances of the problem exactly in polynomial time, particularly when restricted to graphs with bounded treewidth or a bounded number of colors. We also show that a natural approximation algorithm for the problem achieves a performance ratio of 2. We further explore the complexity of the problem in various restricted graph classes and discuss its relationship to other graph properties such as clique number and maximum degree. This work is motivated by its connections to quantum computing and number theory, particularly the concept of quantum number coloring. We also discuss potential applications of the problem in machine learning and combinatorial optimization. Finally, we provide a comprehensive picture of the complexity landscape for the problem in various settings and identify areas for further research. We investigate the effectiveness of angular criteria in suppressing background events, specifically those involving standard model Higgs bosons in association with high-energy jets, compared to hypothetical signals from higgsino pair production at the LHC. Utilizing leading and next-to-leading order calculations within the narrow-width approximation, we analyze the distributions of angular variables under varying jet energies and masses. Our analysis reveals that incorporating angular cuts prior to jet identification can significantly enhance the signal-to-background ratio for higgsino signals at the LHC, particularly in scenarios with neutralino masses below 100 GeV. These results are expected to be valuable for future searches at the high-energy collider, the HL-LHC and its successor. Additionally, we provide a detailed comparison of next-to-leading order and leading order calculations for the standard model Higgs plus jet process at various energies, from 100 GeV to 1000 GeV. We also compare our results with existing parton shower codes and find that our calculations agree with these references. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive comparison of next-to-leading order and leading order calculations for the gluino pair production process at the 14 TeV LHC, focusing on the impact of different jet algorithms and the significance of jet grooming procedures. Our calculations demonstrate that the signal-to-background ratio for the gluino search can be substantially improved by applying jet grooming procedures. These results are expected to be valuable for future searches at the 14 TeV LHC. In computer vision, the success of deep learning has largely been driven by the application of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to various tasks. However, CNNs have significant limitations, such as a lack of interpretability and the need to acquire large labeled training datasets. To address these limitations, Graph Attention Networks (GATs) have been successfully applied to machine learning tasks. We propose a novel approach that integrates GATs with Mean Field inference of Conditional random Fields (CRFs) to develop a highly interpretable deep learning model. The inference process of CRFs is typically computationally intensive, but by using a Mean Field approximation, the method can be significantly accelerated. We have developed a deep learning model that leverages GATs to approximate the Mean Field inference process, resulting in a highly efficient and interpretable deep learning model. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach in image segmentation, yielding state-of-the-art performance. The core of reinforcement learning (RL) lies in an agent learning from interacting with an environment. In this study, we propose a novel approach to RL, which we term active inference RL (AIREL). By incorporating an energy-based model of the environment's state and reward signals into the RL framework, AIREL enables agents to not only learn from their environment but also to modify it to achieve their objectives. This allows agents to navigate towards desired states and outcomes while avoiding detrimental situations. AIREL is based on the active inference framework, which is rooted in Bayesian inference and free energy principles. By optimizing an agent's policy to minimize uncertainty about the world and maximize desired outcomes, AIREL provides a more comprehensive and efficient approach to RL, which we demonstrate through simulated examples and comparative analyses to traditional RL methods. Our findings indicate that AIREL can lead to more efficient learning, robustness to reward signal errors, and increased sample efficiency, which are particularly beneficial in complex, real-world applications. AIREL is an innovative and promising approach to RL, which we believe will contribute to the development of more intelligent and autonomous artificial intelligence systems. Its energy-based models and the Bayesian principles on which it is based offer a unifying framework for understanding various RL mechanisms and their relationships, which we believe will be particularly valuable for researchers interested in this field. AIREL is an open-source library that can be easily integrated into a wide range of RL algorithms and used to address various challenges in real-world applications, which we believe will be of interest to researchers and practitioners in this field. Additionally, AIREL provides a flexible and efficient way to integrate Bayesian priors over policies into RL algorithms, which we believe will be particularly valuable for researchers interested in this field. Finally, AIREL is an important step towards developing more efficient and robust artificial intelligence systems that can not only learn from their environment but also to modify it to achieve their objectives. The $S_8$ parameter, which measures the combination of the matter density and the product of the Hubble constant and the matter density, extracted from galaxy cluster data using the halo model, is a key indicator of the tension between local and global cosmological constraints. We investigated the impact of theoretical and observational limitations on the determination of $S_8$. We discovered that the halo model's assumption that halo concentration depends on the mass of the cluster leads to an inflated $S_8$ value of 0.76, which is 4% higher than the standard value. We further found that the effect of the scatter in the relation between the halo mass and the total gravitational lensing signal is 0.02. We then evaluate the effectiveness of our approach using a set of ground truth images and compare it with existing techniques, demonstrating its superiority in terms of accuracy and performance metrics. Our results also indicate that our proposed method excels at identifying the extent of active ulcer area and accurately classifying image quality. These findings suggest that our proposed method has the potential to revolutionize the monitoring and diagnosis of diabetic foot ulcers, enabling clinicians to make more informed decisions and ultimately leading to a reduction in the risk of amputation and mortality associated with this condition. Our research has significant implications for clinicians and clinicians working in the field of diabetic foot ulcers, and we anticipate that our proposed method will play a crucial role in advancing the monitoring and diagnosis of this complex condition. At the core of numerous geographic information systems and visualizations lies the concept of shortest path distances. While these distances hold immense significance, calculating them accurately is often computationally expensive, prompting the need for a fast approximation technique. To address this challenge, we employ machine learning algorithms, including decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting decision trees, to develop a model capable of approximating the shortest path travel time between two zip code-level locations in the United States. The model is trained on a dataset of approximately 900,000 paths derived from optimal solutions obtained through the use of the L-p highway method. The results demonstrate that the gradient boosting model exhibits the lowest mean absolute error (2.79 minutes), surpassing the performance of random forest (3.05 minutes) and decision tree (4.35 minutes) models. Notably, this model is able to accurately estimate travel times for over 300,000 paths correctly and still maintain a relatively low error rate for the remaining paths. The calculated travel times are then used to estimate the population of a point of interest within a 1-mile radius around a starting location, enabling the generation of a heat map that reflects the population density of the area. The analysis reveals that the population of a point of interest is highly sensitive to the travel time, with the calculated heat map closely approximating the results obtained from a detailed network-based analysis. The origins of neural noise remain unclear, with three primary theories - 
stochasticity in learning processes, variability in neural connections, and 
random fluctuations at the single-neuron level. To distinguish between these 
theories, researchers developed a new experimental approach that tests whether 
noise in neural responses to visual stimuli changes based on the amount of 
stimuli. This approach revealed that the variability of neural responses does 
not change, indicating that the noise is likely inherent to the visual stimuli 
rather than resulting from internal neural circuits. This finding has implications

We investigate the problem of super-resolving a large set of point sources using a single low-resolution image. We model this task as recovering non-negative vectors from linear measurements, where the number of unknown vectors is significantly greater than the number of measurements. This scenario is challenging due to its inherent underdetermination. To address this issue, we propose a fast iterative hard thresholding algorithm, which is a modification of the standard iterative hard thresholding method. By incorporating a simple and efficient projection step, our approach reduces computational complexity at each iteration. We demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm through numerical experiments and establish theoretical guarantees for recovering a fixed number of vectors in this setting. Additionally, we extend our method to super-resolve a large number of vectors when a small subset is known, and provide a proof for recovery in this case. Reinforcement learning algorithms often struggle to effectively evaluate and refine policies using a density ratio test, particularly in large state spaces with high dimensionalities. Our proposed solution addresses this challenge by learning a low-dimensional representation of the state space that accurately reflects the relationship between the true policy and evaluation policy. By doing so, we can apply the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to evaluate policies in a more efficient manner. Building on this approach, we developed a method to improve policies using importance sampling without the need for reward shaping. Our algorithm leverages a learned bias to guide the sampling process, enhancing the efficiency of state transitions and reward computation. Our results demonstrate the superiority of this method in simulated environments and its potential for real-world applications. Notably, this approach can be adapted to a wide range of evaluation and refinement tasks, including estimating the maximum Q-function or predicting cumulative returns. Our experiments show that this adaptation outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in these specific tasks. Overall, our approach offers a versatile solution for general policy evaluation and refinement in large, complex domains. We present ASR2K, a novel speech recognition approach designed for identifying spoken words from languages not supported by existing models. By leveraging text-only knowledge, ASR2K becomes the first speech recognition model to be trained on languages with limited or no available audio. To achieve this, ASR2K utilizes a text-to-image generative model, which creates hypothetical audio examples from given spoken content. These synthesized audio examples are then used to train a second model that predicts spoken words. Through experiments on 10 languages, including 5 languages with no spoken audio, and 5 languages with limited datasets, ASR2K demonstrates its effectiveness in speech recognition tasks. Furthermore, ASR2K is shown to outperform other models in 8 out of 10 languages, achieving results comparable to or superior to those of existing models. In particular, ASR2K achieves a word error rate of 35.8% on the Oriya MK-100 dataset, which is the best result achieved on this dataset so far. We investigate the tradeoff between filter size and precision in approximate set membership, focusing on a key performance metric – support optimality. This measure assesses how closely the support of a filter approaches that of the underlying set, with a smaller metric indicating better performance. We introduce the first adaptive cuckoo filters and evaluate their effectiveness, demonstrating that they achieve optimal support in single-pass applications while outperforming other filters in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ average-time and $\Omega(\log n)$ worst-case precision. Furthermore, we show that adapting the filters enhances worst-case precision. Our findings are supported by experimental evaluations, with single-pass performance rivaling that of the best non-adaptive filters. To address this disparity, we propose a new filter called OptCullOIF, which iteratively filters inputs to achieve optimal support. Experimental results confirm that OptCullOIF surpasses existing filters in worst-case precision. Notably, this filter is adaptable and can be employed in conjunction with single-pass filters to address diverse requirements. Lastly, our work highlights the importance of worst-case analysis in filter design and showcases the benefits of worst-case optimal filters in various scenarios. Our method, which is based on analyzing the symmetry of the network's co-domain, enables us to automatically identify potential symmetry groups. Moreover, we establish specific symmetry groups for certain complex-valued functions, which can serve as a reference for constructing more complex networks with higher symmetries. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of network symmetry, which is essential for building robust and efficient deep learning models. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical applications of this work in the context of invariant training and efficient inference, and showcase its effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Our method is also shown to be superior to existing approaches in tasks such as image classification and signal processing. Overall, this research provides a solid theoretical foundation for building symmetric complex-valued deep learning models. A fractal antenna design called a Fractal Yagi-Uda (FYU) was created and tested, demonstrating enhanced directionality and improved space efficiency. This FYU antenna features 3 main elements: a fractal dipole at its center, surrounded by two fractal parasitic elements that increase its beamwidth by 5.2 degrees and reduce its size by 35% compared to traditional arrays. To assess its resilience, the FYU was exposed to 1000 broken elements - 100 each with 1, 2, or 3 broken elements - while measuring its main lobe's full-width-at-half-max (FWHM). This test showed that the FYU's FWMH remains consistent at approximately 5 degrees for up to three damaged elements, making it 1.6 to 7.5 times more resilient than conventional sparse arrays. Additionally, the research found that the FYU's gain remains stable for up to 100 elements with one broken element each, resulting in a 2.5 dB reduction compared to a fully functioning FYU. To validate these findings, the researchers built a FYU with 100 elements, each with one broken element, and compared its performance to a fully functioning FYU. The results confirmed the theoretical predictions. Lastly, the study analyzed the FYU's gain reduction for different numbers of damaged elements and found a linear relationship described by the equation ΔG = (2.5 ± 0.1) (n/100) dB. This equation can be used to estimate the FYU's gain reduction based on the number of damaged elements. Overall, the study demonstrated the FYU's superior performance in terms of directionality, space efficiency, and resilience to damage. It also showed the feasibility of using fractal antenna design to enhance these performance metrics. This paper investigates the regular behavior of weak and very weak solutions to the degenerate wave equation at the boundary. Building upon prior research, the authors adapted and extended existing non-degenerate case outcomes, first introduced by Fabre and Puel. These pioneering works demonstrated global time regularity and partial space-time regularity for non-degenerate wave equations. Our research builds upon this foundation by broadening these results to accommodate degenerate coefficients, achieving uniform time regularity for all solutions and partial-time space regularity for very weak solutions near the boundary. Additionally, we present new, simplified proofs for the non-degenerate case, unifying and streamlining previous findings. These findings are exemplified through two-dimensional numerical simulations. Our research draws inspiration from the work of Fabre and Puel, the study of the one-dimensional case by Yang and the work of Dupont, Ramanathan and the second author on boundary regularity for one-dimensional degenerate wave equations. These works collectively contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the subject. Finally, the authors provide an English translation of their earlier paper on the subject. References to this translation are denoted in italics (e.g. _[8]_). We introduce a novel approach to unsupervised learning for optical flow estimation, referred to as Self-Teaching Multi-Frame Unsupervised RAFT with Full-Image Warping (SMURF). This model is derived from the established RAFT framework and enhances it by incorporating a multi-frame approach to improve robustness and robustness against occlusions. Diverging from previous methods that utilize flow propagation, our approach involves warping images onto each other. This novel mechanism enables the model to infer the relationship between frames without relying on explicit flow propagation. During training, SMURF is self-supervised by employing a two-way self-supervision strategy that leverages multi-frame consistency and single-frame consistency. This self-supervision strategy allows the model to learn from multi-frame and single-frame flow predictions, thereby enabling it to infer the relationship between frames without relying on explicit flow propagation. Our model is evaluated on various benchmarks, including the KITTI and HumanEva datasets, and outperform previous state-of-the-art models in unsupervised learning for optical flow estimation. Notably, our model achieves a significant reduction in error rate on the KITTI test set, from 0.234 to 0.095, and demonstrates comparable performance to supervised models. This research presents an innovative computational model designed to simulate
multitasking behaviors in artificial agents. By integrating multiple tasks into a
single architecture, this model capitalizes on shared representations to enhance
efficiency and resilience to individual task failures. Through experiments, we
demonstrate that multitasking models can effectively complete tasks even when one
of their assigned tasks becomes unresponsive, either due to a simulated crash or
an intentionally blocked task. Moreover, our findings suggest that a more
extensive training period with multitasking can yield more robust and adaptable
models that remain resilient to individual task failures, a phenomenon akin to
the cognitive reserve in humans, which has been observed in studies of bilingual
individuals with Alzheimer's disease. This research explores the theoretical links
between multitasking, cognitive reserve, and artificial intelligence, and provides
a theoretical framework for the computational model presented. The proposed
model is compared to other prominent neural network architectures, including
single-task neural networks and networks with a shared representation. This
investigation reveals that multitasking models can achieve superior
performance in tasks requiring minimal training data, often outperforming their
single-task and shared-encoder counterparts. The potential applications of this
model extend to various fields, including artificial intelligence, neuroscience,
and psychology, and may also be applied to design more robust and adaptable
artificial intelligence systems. All necessary code and data for the experiments

We introduce Gvnn, a deep learning library for Torch designed to connect the gap between traditional geometric computer vision and modern neural networks. Building upon innovative approaches to reframe classical computer vision problems, neural networks offer enhanced performance and robustness. Focusing on key areas like optical flow, 3D reconstruction, and visual odometry, Gvnn leverages the powerful tools provided by neural networks. Key features of the library include seamless integration with Torch, automatic differentiation for optimization, and a flexible layer system allowing for the incorporation of custom neural layers tailored to specific challenges in geometric computer vision. The repository is available at https://github.com/Navid-Abdi/gvnn. Experiment results demonstrate the efficacy of using neural networks for solving modern geometric vision problems, significantly outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques in optical flow and 3D reconstruction tasks. Notably, Gvnn is the first to successfully tackle 3D reconstruction and visual odometry tasks within the neural network framework. Additionally, this library offers a 3D visual odometry framework for the NVIDIA Jetson TX1, allowing for the deployment of the network on low-cost, portable embedded systems. To facilitate the adoption of neural networks for these applications, Gvnn provides a user-friendly API and a variety of pre-built neural network architectures for tasks such as optical flow, stereo matching, 3D reconstruction, and visual odomy. Furthermore, users can easily create their own neural network architectures by extending the library's layer set. A significant number of IoT users are eager to outsource their computations to nearby IoT devices, but current solutions either rely on intermediaries or lack privacy. Our research introduces Self-Serviced IoT (S2IoT), a decentralized IoT platform that enables users to offload computations to nearby IoT devices without requiring intermediaries. S2IoT allows users to select their preferred IoT devices, ensuring maximum privacy. We present a novel solution leveraging edge computing and blockchain technology to create a secure and efficient marketplace where users and IoT devices interact directly. Our solution incorporates a robust incentive mechanism that fairly rewards IoT devices for their resources and computational power. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate S2IoT's ability to offer secure, efficient, and privacy-enhanced offloading services, with significant performance gains compared to existing solutions. Furthermore, our solution ensures the satisfaction of various real-world use cases, such as private data analysis, machine learning, and augmented reality. These use cases can now be fully realized, thanks to S2IoT's ability to provide secure and direct IoT offloading services. Our research has been successfully implemented on a private blockchain testnet, with promising results. The code for our solution is available on GitHub. https://github.com/ParagSankpal/S2IoT. The emerging field of optimal transport offers a unified approach to comparing and analyzing probability measures, with significant implications in machine learning and data science. However, solving optimal transport problems with high-dimensional data is computationally challenging, motivating the development of low-rank optimal transport methods. Despite their potential for scalability, low-rank optimal transport methods often produce biased solutions due to their relaxed formulations. In response, we introduce a family of algorithms that integrate low-rank relaxation with local refinement techniques, enabling us to derive error bounds for the approximation of optimal transport maps and the estimation of low-rank transport maps. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to remove the bias associated with estimated transport maps using kernel smoothing, and we show that our methods can be efficiently implemented using stochastic optimization techniques. The proposed methods are then empirically evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets, with applications in clustering, anomaly detection, and image processing. In particular, we show that our methods can effectively address the curse of dimensionality and achieve competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods in image denoising tasks. In comparison with existing low-rank transport methods, our approach yields higher-quality transport maps, both in terms of their accuracy and their ability to produce unbiased estimates. The goal of algorithmic fairness is to ensure that algorithms treat individuals fairly and equally, without regard for sensitive attributes like their gender or racial background. Typically, this objective is pursued by training a classifier while minimizing the disparity between different groups under review. In contrast, we propose a new method that focuses on learning a fair image representation. We do this by training a neural network while optimizing a combination function that aims to minimize the disparity across groups and maximize the inter-group variation. Furthermore, we show that our fair representation can be used to generate adversarial examples that challenge the fairness of biased classifiers. Glacier calving fronts play a key role in understanding glacier dynamics, with accurate measurement of their position crucial for climate change research. Despite the complexity of this task, several deep learning approaches have been developed to identify glacier fronts in satellite imagery. This study introduces a new method, the Bayesian U-Net, which leverages a probabilistic approach to improve segmentation accuracy. By incorporating uncertainty estimation, the Bayesian U-Net enables the calculation of posterior probabilities for segmentation predictions, which can then be translated into multiple possible segmentations. We evaluate the performance of the Bayesian U-Net on three distinct glacier datasets and find that it outperforms comparable models on satellite imagery with complex features and varying image quality. Moreover, the Bayesian U-Net's uncertainty estimates enable the detection of potential errors in the segmentation process, which can then be verified using additional information. Our results suggest that the Bayesian U-Net's probabilistic design enhances the reliability of segmentation outcomes, making it a valuable tool for monitoring glacier dynamics. This paper introduces a novel reinforcement learning method that merges the strengths of model-based and model-free approaches. Model-based techniques utilizing the Model-Prior Optimizer (MPC) have shown promise in efficiently learning optimal policies for complex environments with high-dimensional spaces, albeit with slower learning speeds compared to model-free methods. Conversely, model-free methods like the Actor-Critic Algorithm (ACA) offer faster learning but may struggle in environments with sparse rewards. To address this disparity, our research presents the MPC-ACA algorithm, a hybrid method that leverages the MPC's ability to develop accurate dynamics models and the ACA's fast learning capabilities. By combining the MPC's policy and reward functions with the ACA's learning algorithm, MPC-ACA bridges the performance gap between efficient optimization and fast learning. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of MPC-ACA in achieving optimal performance using fewer samples on challenging continuous control tasks with sparse rewards, outpacing state-of-the-art methods like ACA and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG). Moreover, our results show that MPC-ACA can efficiently learn optimal policies for complex tasks with sparse rewards, effectively bridging the performance gap between efficient optimization and fast learning. The surge in the use of Computer Vision techniques in Cellular Electron Microscopy (CEM) data analysis is rapidly increasing. This growing interest is largely attributed to the development of advanced imaging techniques such as Serial Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Electron Tomography (ETM), which generate vast amounts of complex data. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the current state of AIA in large-scale CEM data analysis. The survey covers key deep learning research in the last five years, categorizing it into four areas: image segmentation, cell reconstruction, pattern recognition, and volume analysis. The ability to communicate between different contexts of a web application is a fundamental aspect of the web architecture. This functionality is particularly significant in modern web browsers, as it enables the seamless execution of web applications across various platforms. Despite its importance, cross-context communication in web browsers poses significant challenges due to the need for data transfer and synchronization. In this research, we present a classification framework for cross-context communication in web browsers, highlighting its key characteristics and requirements. We also identify existing solutions that address these requirements, with the ultimate goal of facilitating the development of web browsers that can efficiently handle complex web applications. This work is intended to serve as a foundation for further research in the field of cross-context communication in web browsers.

Call graph analysis, a fundamental tool in software development, has been extensively researched to improve software performance. However, the changing call graphs of software versions pose a significant challenge in developing advanced analysis tools. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach to call graph evolution analytics, utilizing a data structure that tracks call graph changes between version series of evolving software systems. This approach enables the identification of dynamic call graph changes, computation of graph-based metrics, and generation of a summary report for in-depth analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to six diverse open-source Java projects and presenting the results in a publicly accessible tool. The accompanying code and dataset are available for further research. The proposed analytics provide valuable insights into call graph evolution, which can be leveraged to develop innovative tools for software optimization. Our research aims to facilitate the development of advanced call graph analysis tools that address the growing challenges of modern software development. A novel algorithm has been developed for estimating a multivariate mixing distribution under the assumption that the data are generated by an independent mixture model with an unknown number of identically distributed components. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, a significant challenge is path instability, 
caused by other agents' unpredictable policies. To address this issue, we 
introduce "satisficing paths" - a type of policy that remains consistent under 
varying conditions. We establish that in multi-agent Markov games, a 
satisficing path exists and can be derived from a specific class of policies known 
as normal-form Nash mixed strategies. Furthermore, we show that these strategies 
are resilient to changes in other agents' policies and can be learned through 
averaging over the limit of these strategies. Our findings also reveal that in 
convergent normal-form games, a unique fixed point exists and can be achieved by 
utilizing a variant of the independent Q-learning algorithm. This result provides 
a theoretical foundation for the convergence of independent Q-learning in such games. 
Moreover, simulations confirm that normal-form policies exhibit a high degree of 
satisficing capability, while in contrast, state-space policies are prone to 
instability. Our study also highlights the importance of choosing the right state 
space representation to achieve a stable learning experience. Overall, our research 
offers a new perspective for analyzing and addressing the challenge of path 
instability in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Additionally, it provides a 
theoretical basis for implementing decentralized learning in convergent games. By 
leveraging the properties of satisficing paths, practitioners can now better manage 
the impact of other agents' policies on their agents' learning processes. This 
theoretical breakthrough opens up new avenues for addressing the complexity of 
multi-agent reinforcement learning. To facilitate further research, a 
companion repository is provided with the relevant code and data. This repository 
includes implementations of the fixed point algorithm, the Q-learning variant, and 
numerous simulation scenarios. Additionally, the repository contains visualizations 
of the properties of state-space and normal-form policies, while also providing 
detailed documentation. This resource is designed to support researchers and 
practitioners in exploring the properties of satisficing paths and their practical 
applications in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Finally, we identify 
potential directions for future research and outline the challenges that still 
need to be addressed. Our research has been made possible through the support of the

This paper explores a technique known as renormalized importance sampling, also referred to as renormalized importance sampling, which is based on the Gumbel-max trick. Utilized in a broad spectrum of applications, the Gumbel-max trick has the ability to extract the most likely sample from a categorical distribution modified by a learnable inductive bias. Diverging from the traditional approach of selecting samples directly from a distribution modified by an inductive bias, renormalized importance sampling involves importance sampling a proposal distribution, normalizing the samples, and then selecting the sample with the highest normalized value. This work is intended to serve as a comprehensive introduction to renormalized importance sampling and is expected to be a valuable resource for machine learning researchers. The widespread adoption of deep learning techniques in natural language processing has been hindered by the scarcity of suitable training data. In response to this challenge, researchers have developed mixed-file data sets that offer a more accessible and efficient alternative to traditional text-based corpora. This study introduces NapierOne, a large mixed-file data set comprising 1.5 million records and 7 million pages of both structured and unstructured content. By drawing inspiration from GovdocsOne, NapierOne is designed to support the development of advanced machine learning models for data extraction and document understanding. An in-depth analysis of the data reveals its complex nature, with a complex hierarchy of page layouts and varied content types. To demonstrate the effectiveness of NapierOne, a baseline model is trained using the HuggingFace transformer architecture, with a linear weight aggregator, and shown to achieve impressive performance on key tasks. The results indicate that the model has a high capacity for extracting relevant information from the data, with a classification accuracy of 0.95 and a precision of 0.90. Monocular 3D object detection is a complex task in computer vision that involves estimating the properties of 3D bounding boxes from single-image projections. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a straightforward yet effective approach that utilizes image depth information through a dynamic message propagation mechanism. Our method features a two-branch architecture, where one branch processes the depth map and the other focuses on the image. By integrating these two components, we enable the propagation of depth information across different object levels, thus enhancing the detection performance. Our approach is easy to implement, efficient, and can be applied to various monocular 3D object detection methods. Experiments demonstrate its effectiveness on prominent benchmarks, KITTI and Waymo Open Dataset, achieving top results in both 3D bird's-eye view and 3D object detection. A safety supervisor is a crucial component that monitors a robot's or system's safety-critical functions and activates protective measures to prevent harm. The design of such supervisors involves creating a complex system that integrates sensors, sensors' uncertainty, safety protocols, uncertainty estimation, and protective measures. 

Given the system's inherent complexity, verifying its correctness is a significant challenge, and traditional verification methods often fall short due to time constraints and the complexity of systems. 

This paper introduces a novel verification method that leverages model checking to validate the correctness of safety supervisors. The method enables the synthesis of supervisor designs and the creation of self-testing mechanisms that can be executed on the system. 

The proposed method is demonstrated on a robot navigation system, and it successfully identifies and confirms the system's safety-critical functions, providing assurance of correct supervisor design. The method's effectiveness is further highlighted by its application to a real-world industrial system. 

This research showcases the potential of verification in synthesizing reliable safety supervisors, and it opens up new possibilities for the field of verification in safety-critical systems. The method's source code is publicly available.

Additionally, the method is applied to estimate and classify functional data observed in geographical coordinates. Moreover, the method is used to analyze the temporal and spatial patterns of air pollution in Mexico City. Self-supervised learning (SSL) has recently achieved impressive performance in various tasks, but it remains understudied in the context of dataset imbalance. In this paper, we investigate the effects of dataset imbalance on SSL methods, focusing on the impact of class distribution discrepancy. We examine the performance of three SSL methods on the CIFAR-100 dataset, modified to have different levels of imbalance. Our results show that SSL methods exhibit greater resilience to dataset imbalance compared to supervised learning (SL) methods. Notably, SSL methods maintain relatively stable performance even with extreme imbalance, whereas SL methods suffer significantly. We also observe that the SSL training process can effectively mitigate imbalance effects. In contrast to existing literature, our findings highlight the robustness of SSL to imbalance and suggest its potential as a strategy to mitigate imbalance, offering a promising approach for handling imbalanced datasets. This study delves into the feasibility of condensing a system's adjustable settings, such as those related to data processing and storage, into a condensed form at compile time. Our results indicate that Chord's specialization can significantly outperform the original system, with speedups of up to 3.49. We also examine the influence of Chord's design decisions on its performance and identify opportunities for future enhancements aimed at further improving its specialization capabilities. where the probability of adding new branches depends on the number of existing

as a product of two functions, one dependent on the number of branches and the

can be expressed as a sum over a certain type of random walk.  The results are

Modern bus fleets are equipped with advanced tracking systems that provide detailed location data, allowing transportation researchers to gain valuable insights. Our research project focuses on leveraging this data to improve the reliability of public transportation by analyzing the behavior of buses. Our study used a dataset of over 1.5 million GPS readings for 170,000 unique bus journeys in Warsaw, Poland. Our findings demonstrate that certain machine learning models can achieve high accuracy in predicting delays, with some achieving up to 90% accuracy. Our results also show that the decision tree (DT) model outperformed others, providing the best balance of accuracy and complexity. Additionally, our analysis revealed that the time of the day and the bus driver's experience are crucial factors influencing bus behavior, with drivers' experience having a significant impact on prediction accuracy. Neutrinos possess an inherent property called flavor instability due to their unique interactions. In certain conditions, such as when neutrinos are actively being produced, this flavor instability can manifest as a change in their relative abundance, which in turn affects the distribution of neutrino flavors in space. Researchers have proposed metrics to quantify this flavor instability but their application is limited to specific simulations. A new approach has been developed that can evaluate and compare the level of flavor instability in space without relying on a particular method, known as the Eulerian framework. This new approach has been tested on two specific simulations of a neutron star merger and the results show that flavor instability occurs in areas with high neutrino production rates, such as the surface of an accretion disk, where neutrinos are actively being emitted. In contrast, regions with lower neutrino production, such as the disk's midplane, do not experience significant flavor instability. Furthermore, differences in how the simulations are set up do not appear to have a significant impact on the level of flavor instability observed. A comparison of the proposed metric with existing metrics shows that they yield consistent results, supporting the use of this new approach for evaluating flavor instability in a wider range of simulations. In the future, this new approach can be applied to simulations of other astrophysical phenomena, such as those involving black holes or neutron stars. This paper explores the application of second-order sensitivity analysis to a specific type of bilevel optimization problem, specifically Dantzig-Dantzig reformulation. A novel computational method is developed to estimate the sensitivity of the lower-level problem with respect to the upper-level problem's parameters. By utilizing this analysis, a novel second-order approximation of the upper-level problem's objective function is created, leading to the derivation of two new second-order approximations. These approximations enable the creation of two new models: a two-stage stochastic program with probabilistic second-order information and a bilevel optimization model with second-order information on the lower level. A computational study demonstrates the benefits of these novel models in solving real-world inventory and supply chain planning problems. Ultimately, the proposed models have been shown to be more effective in solving large-scale problems within reasonable computational times. A software tool has been created to facilitate the implementation and solution of these novel models. Additionally, the authors provide a comprehensive description of the underlying mathematical framework, including the derivation of key mathematical results. These results are crucial in the development of the proposed models. A notable aspect of this work is its application of second-order sensitivity analysis to a specific class of bilevel optimization problems, a mathematical concept that has not been previously explored in the literature. We introduce HSC4D, a novel dataset for capturing three-dimensional human movements
in real-world environments. Comprising 1.3 terabytes of data from 1,444 participants
engaging in 1,229 diverse activities, HSC4D combines data from wearable sensors,
high-definition video cameras, and 3D LiDAR scanners to provide comprehensive
information about human movements. By integrating data from various sources,
HSC4D enables researchers to track detailed movements, including body and limb
positions, to study human dynamics and interactions with their environment.
The large-scale HSC4D dataset is designed to facilitate various applications
such as human motion analysis, action recognition, and social human behavior
understanding, offering a rich platform for computer vision researchers. We have
made HSC4D available online for public access. We have also demonstrated the
dataset's utility through two case studies, one of which involved 3D human pose
estimation using deep learning, and the other involved 3D scene reconstruction
using LiDAR data. Our experiments on these case studies have shown promising results,
underscoring the value of HSC4D as a benchmark for future research. We have
also provided an analysis of the dataset's characteristics and its potential
applications. As far as we know, HSC4D is the largest publicly available dataset
for capturing human movements in 3D. We have made our HSC4D dataset available
at https://hsc4d.cs.cmu.edu. Our code and models will be released in the future.

The primary objective of saliency detection is to identify the most relevant regions in an image that convey the main message. Despite the success of fully-supervised approaches in this field, limited attention has been paid to weakly-supervised methods. This paper introduces a novel weakly-supervised approach called Saliency Object Subitizing (SOS), which is based on object counting, to generate precise salient object maps from images with only category-level annotations. SOS is unique as it is the first method to achieve fully weakly-supervised Saliency Detection. This is achieved by training a network to identify salient objects through two subtasks: object detection and object counting. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SOS, which outperforms current state-of-the-art weakly-supervised methods in three benchmark datasets. Furthermore, SOS also excels in fully-supervised approaches in terms of the average f-score on the Viper dataset. This paper's code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenChaoGong/SOS. This paper presents a novel monocular approach to generate 3D semantic maps from street view images. To achieve this, we propose a hierarchical birds-eye-view segmentation network, ViT-BEVSeg, which integrates a vision transformer encoder to capture global context and a transformer encoder to extract local details. By employing a patch-based architecture, we generate semantic maps that accurately reflect the ground truth at a lower resolution while preserving a larger field of view. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method, yielding state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI-360 and nuScenes datasets. Moreover, we provide a detailed ablation study to validate every component of our network. To further advance the field, we release our source code and model weights on GitHub for public access. One widely used segmentation method is change-point detection, particularly for time series with significant shifts in the mean. We propose a new approach that leverages factor vector autoregressives for time series segmentation. Factor vector autoregressives can capture interdependencies between time series while accounting for changes in the mean and common trends through factor segmentation. We develop a computational algorithm to infer both change and factor segmentation points and provide theoretical guarantees for our method's consistency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using simulations and real-world examples, including stock market analysis. Our method is implemented in the R package tvfba. Analysis of stock price data reveals that factor segmentation often aligns with economic sector categorization, and our approach can detect shifts in the common trend and sector-level dynamics. The proposed method can be useful for identifying sectors with distinct short-term and long-term dynamics in financial time series.
